name: Newari / Kathmandu Newari
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_quote: [Friedman, Kansakar, Tuladhar & Hale 1983:38] Some rules operate only in word-final position, others word-initially, and still others apply to what we refer to as strong syllables. Strong syllables are morphologically defined as stem-initial syllables, Thus, in a disyllabic word without affixes or complex internal morphology, the first syllable is strong and the second syllable is weak (... 'oil', ... 'easy', ... 'soon'). The negative prefix is not a stem, thus in verbs with negative prefixes the second syllable is strong (/ma-py~/ 'd[o]es not give', /ma-cuy/ 'did not sell well'). In words having suffixes but no prefixes, the first syllable is strong (/ya.ta/ 'he did it' ...). In numeral classifier constructions, both the numeral and the classifier behave as stems, and both are strong (... 'four times'). [p.44] /ae/ is otherwise realized in stressed syllables as [...] [Kansakar 1980:12-14] ... also to distinguish 'stressed' or 'strong' positions within the word from 'unstressed' or 'weak' positions. For example, the two syllables in /nene/ 'to ask' are phonetically quite distinct. ... (4) ... palatalization occurs in syllables with initial consonants which occupy 'strong' positions within a word (word-initial or the initial syllable of a word within a compound) [Kansakar 1977:1] it is my impression that Newari has a distinct stress-timed rhythm although stress as a phonetic feature is not linguistically significant at the word-level in the language.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: newa1246 (Kathmandu Valley Newari) is not in the catalog. Three title hits. Two are Genetti's Dolakha Newar prosody papers (Genetti & Slater 2004, Himalayan Linguistics, doi 10.5070/H91122520, downloaded open from eScholarship; Genetti 2007 SEALS XIII, downloaded open from sealang.net, image-only, pp. 53-55 scanned): both concern a different, mutually unintelligible variety (Dolakha, Glottolog dolk1238) and treat intonation units and phrase-level 'prosodic accent', not word stress; Genetti & Slater fn. 5 defers to Kansakar 1977 for the Kathmandu dialect. The one relevant item, Kansakar 1977 'Rhythm and intonation in colloquial Newari' (CNAS 5(1): 1-14; already held by the project from Digital Himalaya, scanned), is a native-speaker first-hand statement: stress 'is not linguistically significant at the word-level' (p. 1), no lexical tone (p. 5), prominence is foot/utterance-level ('emphatic stress' on the focused word, falling vs rising tunes). Nothing read gives a word-stress position for Kathmandu Newari; the best available coding is 'no lexical stress, phrasal prominence'. For comparison the on-disk Genetti 2007 Dolakha grammar (pp. 64-68) reports predictable, non-phonemic first-syllable prominence in isolation. Not obtained (per the earlier reading's list of works to obtain): Hale & Hale 1969 / Hale 1970 Newari phonemic summary in Hale & Pike, Tone systems of Tibeto-Burman languages of Nepal (Google Books snippet mentions 'stress and rhythm within the stress group'), Kansakar's 1979/80 Tribhuvan PhD 'A generative phonology of Kathmandu Newari', Hale & Shrestha 2006 (LINCOM), Hargreaves 2003/2017 (Routledge) -- these, not the three search hits, are where a fuller Kathmandu word-stress statement would be; Hale & Pike 1970 and Kansakar's thesis are the high-priority acquisitions. New files and. downloads were done via Crossref API, eScholarship and sealang.net directly.

new_statements.quote: [p.1] ... it is my impression that Newari has a distinct stress-timed rhythm although stress as a phonetic feature is not linguistically significant at the word-level in the language. [p.3] (a) Each foot of an utterance constitute the rhythmic unit, and that the structure of a foot normally consists of salient and weak syllables. (b) When each sentence is said in normal speed the stressed or salient syllable is more prominent or longer than the weak or unstressed syllable. [p.6] Although Newari does not have contrastive lexical tone, its intonation pattern must be analyzed in terms of pitch levels and pitch movements ... [fn.1, p.13] Newari as spoken in Kathmandu is considered to be the standard dialect ...
new_statements.citation: Kansakar, Tej R. 1977. Rhythm and intonation in colloquial Newari. Contributions to Nepalese Studies (CNAS, Tribhuvan University) 5(1): 1-14.
new_statements.locator: p.1 (sec. 1 Introduction), with p.3 (1.2, conclusions a-b), p.6 (2.1) and footnote 1, p.13
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (page scan) and. All four quoted pieces are at the stated locators and verbatim (only difference: the line-break hyphen in 'word-/level' on p.1): p.1 '..it is my impression that Newari has a distinct stress-timed rhythm although stress as a phonetic feature is not linguistically significant at the word-level in the language.'; p.3 conclusions (a) and (b) exactly as quoted; p.6 'Although Newari does not have contrastive lexical tone, its intonation pattern must be analyzed in terms of pitch levels and pitch movements..'; fn.1 p.13 'Newari as spoken in Kathmandu is considered to be the standard dialect..'. On the identity of the variety: Kansakar analys…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Standard (Kathmandu) Newari the author, a native-speaker phonologist, states that stress is not linguistically significant (non-contrastive) at the word level; prominence is described only as a property of rhythmic feet (salient + weak syllables, salient syllable longer) and of sentence intonation/emphasis, i.e. stress-timed rhythm without a stated word-level stress position. No lexical tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress; 'silent stress' (pause) is treated as part of the utterance rhythm (fn.5).
new_statements.exceptions: None at word level; emphatic (double-marked) stress on a word affects the sentence-final pitch movement (p.12). Author flags the analysis as tentative, based on his own recorded speech ('The North Wind and the Sun').
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about connected speech (feet, utterances) and explicitly denies word-level significance; it gives no default position for citation forms. For the closely related but separate Glottolog language Dolakha Newar (east2773) Genetti 2007:64-68 reports predictable first-syllable prominence cued by pitch, low functional load; Hale 1970 analysed Kathmandu Newari with a 'stress group' unit (snippet only) and may state a position.
new_statements.identity_note: Kansakar 1977 describes 'Standard Newari', i.e. Newari as spoken in Kathmandu (his own speech; fn.1), = Glottolog newa1246 (Kathmandu-Patan dialect kath1254). Joshi 1984 is the Bhaktapur dialect (also under newa1246) and is silent on stress. The explicit initial-stress statements found (Genetti 1994, 2007) are for Dolakha Newar, a separate Glottolog language (Eastern Newari east2773 / dolk1238), and Shrestha 2010's vague 'word boundary' stress remark is for Pahari Newar (paha1257); neither should be entered under newa1246.

new_statements.quote: it is my impression that Newari has a distinct stress-timed rhythm although stress as a phonetic feature is not linguistically significant at the word-level in the language.
new_statements.citation: Kansakar, Tej Ratna. 1977. Rhythm and intonation in colloquial Newari. Contributions to Nepalese Studies 5(1): 1-14.
new_statements.locator: p. 1, sec. 1 Introduction (last paragraph before fn. 1); supporting: p. 5 sec. 2, p. 7 sec. 2.2, fn. 1 p. 13
new_statements.reading: Kathmandu (Standard) Newari has no linguistically significant word-level stress and no lexical tone (p. 5); prominence is a property of the foot and the utterance (stress-timed rhythm, 'emphatic stress' on the focused word, two intonation tunes). A native-speaker phonetician's first-hand statement, but explicitly impressionistic and based on a single read text. No word-stress position can be coded from it; the appropriate coding would be 'no lexical stress / stress not significant at word level, prominence phrasal'. Comparison only: Dolakha Newar (Genetti 2007 grammar pp. 64-68) has predictable initial-syllable prominence in isolation, low functional load, obscured by intonation.

[p.3] (a) Each foot of an utterance constitute the rhythmic unit, and that the structure of a foot normally consists of salient and weak syllables. (b) When each sentence is said in normal speed the stressed or salient syllable is more prominent or longer than the weak or unstressed syllable. sources.locator: p.1 (sec. 1 Introduction), with p.3 (1.2, conclusions a-b), p.6 (2.1) and footnote 1, p.13
sources.note: p.1: Newari (Standard = Kathmandu, author's own speech) has a stress-timed rhythm but 'stress as a phonetic feature is not linguistically significant at the word-level'; feet consist of salient + weak syllables, salient syllable longer/more prominent (p.3); no contrastive lexical tone (pp.5-6); sentence intonation interacts with position of the (emphatically) stressed word (p.12). No rule for which syllable of a word is salient.
